summary: This program builds a dictionary where each key is a student's name and each value is a list of the classes that student takes at a magic academy. It then loops through the dictionary and prints one tidy line per student.

lines.text: The opening brace starts a dictionary literal. Because the entries are long, they are spread over several lines, which Python allows until the matching closing brace appears.
This is one key-value pair: the key is the string "Sally" and the value is a list of four course names. Storing a list as a value is what lets a single key hold many pieces of related data.
The final entry has no trailing comma before the closing brace, though Python would accept one there too.
The `items()` method hands back each pair as a key and a value together, so `student` holds the name and `classes` holds that student's list on every pass through the loop.
`', '.join(classes)` glues the list items into one string separated by commas, which reads far better than printing the raw list with its brackets and quotes.
